blocks.text: 3. Functions of a complex variable, limits, and continuity

segments.text: A complex function w = f(z) maps points in one complex plane to points in another; limits and continuity are defined analogously to the real case, but because z can approach a point from infinitely many directions in the plane (not just from the left or right, as on the real line), the limit must agree along every possible path of approach — a substantially stronger requirement than in single-variable real calculus.

items.text: The complex plane represents complex numbers geometrically; polar/exponential form (via Euler’s formula) dramatically simplifies multiplication, powers (De Moivre’s theorem), and root-finding compared to rectangular form.
Complex limits must agree along every possible path of approach in the plane, a stronger condition than real-variable limits along a line.
The Cauchy–Riemann equations are the defining condition for analyticity, and force both the real and imaginary parts of an analytic function to satisfy Laplace’s equation.

Cauchy’s integral theorem (contour integral of an analytic function is zero) and the Cauchy integral formula (boundary values determine all interior values) are foundational, real-variable-calculus-defying results.
The residue theorem converts contour integration into identifying singularities and summing their residues, a powerful technique also used to evaluate otherwise difficult real integrals.
